claims.text: The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy has a BCC-based matrix.
The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase and nominally homogeneous.
Aging at 600–800 °C can produce a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates in HfNbTaTiZr.
The engineered precipitates have a coefficient of thermal expansion different from that of the BCC matrix.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the precipitates and matrix generates localized internal stress fields during thermal cycling.
Precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction govern the magnitude and spatial distribution of the mismatch stresses.
Precipitates can influence the alloy's mechanical behavior.
Precipitate-induced internal stresses modify dislocation dynamics under mechanical loading.
Precipitate-induced internal stresses modify microstructural evolution under mechanical loading.
The same precipitate-induced stress field can jointly explain tensile creep, cold-work hardening, and temperature-dependent elastic moduli.
Relative to the baseline, the tailored alloy will have a reduced tensile creep rate near 1250 °C because the internal stress field opposes dislocation motion.
Relative to the baseline, the tailored alloy will exhibit enhanced or more consistent elastic-modulus behavior from 293 to 1100 K.
Relative to the baseline, the tailored alloy will exhibit a modified strain-hardening response during cold work.
The proposed controlled comparison uses an engineered aged group and an as-cast or conventionally aged control lacking the engineered precipitate distribution.
The proposed response boundaries are aging at 600–800 °C, creep testing near 1250 °C, and elastic-modulus measurements over 293–1100 K.
Grain-boundary effects and interstitial impurities may also contribute to the observed behavior.
